props.title: Blood for Dracula
props.initialSlug: Weakened Dracula hunts virgin blood in Italy

sections.content: Paul Morrissey's **Blood for Dracula** (1974) reimagines vampire mythology through an art-house lens, delivering a darkly comic take on the Count's legacy. Following Andy Warhol's Factory aesthetic, the film stands in stark contrast to Hammer Horror's gothic **Dracula** (1958) or the expressionist **Nosferatu** (1922). Udo Kier's sickly, emaciated Count desperately searches Italy for virgin blood, creating a meditation on purity, capitalism, and decay that feels more Pasolini than Stoker.

sections.content: The film's exploitation elements mask deeper commentary on class warfare and religious hypocrisy. Joe Dallesandro's communist handyman represents working-class virility opposing aristocratic parasitism. This political subtext aligns with contemporary European art films like **The Conformist** (1970) and **Last Tango in Paris** (1972), which similarly explored power dynamics through sexuality.

Morrissey's direction emphasizes artifice and theatricality, drawing from both Warhol's experimental films and European art cinema. The excessive gore and sexual content push boundaries while serving the film's satirical aims. This approach influenced later vampire deconstructions like **The Hunger** (1983) and **Only Lovers Left Alive** (2013). SUBHEAD: Sexual Politics and Power Dynamics

movies.title: The Hunger
movies.slug: Tony Scott's stylish vampire film starring David Bowie and Catherine Deneuve as immortal lovers

sections.content: The film's treatment of virginity and blood purity serves as pointed commentary on Catholic dogma and aristocratic obsession with bloodlines. Like Pier Paolo Pasolini's **Salò** (1975) and Jean-Luc Godard's **Weekend** (1967), Morrissey uses shocking content to critique bourgeois values. The Count's deterioration parallels the decay of European nobility.

The film's legacy can be traced through later arthouse horror films like **Trouble Every Day** (2001) and **Let the Right One In** (2008), which similarly use vampire mythology to explore sexuality and power. Kier's performance as the enfeebled Count influenced portrayals of vampires as tragic rather than purely monstrous figures.
